questions.stem: Which of the three muscle tissue types is under voluntary (conscious) control?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is stimulated consciously by the nervous system to produce movement at joints. Cardiac and smooth muscle are both involuntary.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Smooth muscle is characteristically found in:
options: The walls of hollow organs, blood vessels, and respiratory passageways
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle forms the walls of hollow organs (stomach, intestines, bladder), blood vessels, and airways, where it moves contents and regulates lumen diameter.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Compared with skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle is described as:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but only lightly so, reflecting its less densely organized sarcomere arrangement.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Multinucleated muscle cells are a feature of:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, cylindrical, and multinucleated, arising from developmental mitosis without cytoplasmic division. Cardiac cells have one (occasionally two) nuclei; smooth cells have one.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Which muscle type fatigues rapidly?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle contracts and relaxes rapidly but fatigues quickly. Cardiac and smooth muscle are built for sustained, rhythmic, or prolonged activity without fatigue.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle is classified as which type of control?
questions.explanation: The heart generates its own electrical impulses (autorhythmicity), though the autonomic nervous system and hormones modify rate and force. Contraction is involuntary.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Wavelike (peristaltic) contractions that move substances through hollow organs are a function of:
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is the hallmark of smooth muscle, propelling contents along the GI tract and other tubular organs.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle produces body movement by:
options: Attaching to bones and acting across joints
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle attaches to bones; its voluntary contractions pull on bones to produce movement at joints.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: A spindle-shaped cell, tapered at each end with a single central nucleus, describes:
questions.explanation: The smooth muscle cell is spindle-shaped with tapered ends and one central nucleus — markedly different from branched cardiac cells or long multinucleated skeletal fibers.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Cardiac myocytes are morphologically described as:
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are short, branched cells — a design that, with intercalated discs, creates a connected network capable of synchronized contraction.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Intercalated discs are found exclusively in:
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs — containing desmosomes and gap junctions — are the specialized junctions connecting cardiac myocytes; they do not exist in skeletal or smooth muscle.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: The ability of muscle to generate its own electrical impulses (autorhythmicity) is a property of:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is self-excitatory: impulses arise within the muscle itself (SA node). Skeletal muscle requires nerve stimulation, and smooth muscle responds to nerves, hormones, and local factors.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Which muscle type constitutes the largest proportion of the body's muscle tissue?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle constitutes the largest proportion of the body's muscle mass, consistent with its role in posture and movement.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: The single central nucleus of a smooth muscle cell sits within a cell that is:
questions.explanation: The classic smooth muscle morphology is a spindle (fusiform) shape, tapered at each end, with a single central nucleus.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Heavy striations in skeletal muscle reflect:
options: The highly organized arrangement of actin and myosin into sarcomeres
questions.explanation: Striations are the visual signature of sarcomeres: precisely aligned thick and thin filaments. Skeletal muscle is heavily striated because of this ordered arrangement.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Smooth muscle responds to which of the following stimuli?
options: Nerve impulses, hormones, and other local stimuli
questions.explanation: As an involuntary muscle, smooth muscle is regulated by autonomic nerves, circulating hormones, and local chemical factors (e.g., metabolites, stretch).
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle activity is modified by:
options: The autonomic nervous system and hormones
questions.explanation: Although the heart initiates its own impulses, the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic/parasympathetic) and hormones (e.g., epinephrine, thyroid hormone) modify rate and contractile force.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Multiple nuclei per skeletal muscle fiber result from:
options: Repeated mitosis during development without cytoplasmic (cytokinetic) division
Nuclear migration from satellite cells in adults
questions.explanation: During development, skeletal muscle cells undergo mitosis without cytoplasmic division, producing long multinucleated fibers.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: The myometrium of the uterus is composed of:
options: A mixture of all three types
questions.explanation: The uterus, like other hollow organs, is lined with smooth muscle capable of slow, powerful, sustained contractions coordinated by hormones.
tags: Muscle Tissue Types — Comparative Structure and Function

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle is located in:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is confined to the myocardium, the muscular wall of the heart. ---

questions.stem: The contraction characteristics of smooth muscle are best described as:
options: Slow and sustained, able to remain contracted for long periods
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle contracts slowly and can maintain contraction for extended periods without fatigue — ideal for vascular tone, sphincter control, and organ wall function.

questions.stem: Smooth muscle is non-striated because:
options: Its actin and myosin are not arranged in a regular sarcomere pattern
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle contains actin and myosin, but they are not organized into repeating sarcomere units; hence no visible striations.

questions.stem: Within blood vessels, vascular smooth muscle primarily functions to:
options: Pump blood forward like a ventricle
Regulate the diameter (caliber) of the vessel lumen
Anchor the vessel to surrounding tissue
questions.explanation: Vascular smooth muscle adjusts vessel caliber: constriction narrows the lumen, relaxation widens it — regulating flow distribution and blood pressure.

questions.stem: The mechanism by which smooth muscle moves substances through hollow organs is:
questions.explanation: Sequential wavelike contractions (peristalsis) propel contents along tubular organs — the signature function of smooth muscle in the gut and ureters.

questions.stem: Sustained smooth muscle tone in the arterioles contributes directly to:
questions.explanation: Arteriolar tone sets systemic vascular resistance; constriction raises blood pressure, and relaxation lowers it.

questions.stem: Which statement about smooth muscle striations is correct?
options: Smooth muscle has the heaviest striations of the three types
Smooth muscle striations appear only during systole
questions.explanation: Because its myofilaments are not organized into sarcomeres, smooth muscle shows no striations on microscopy.

questions.stem: In the respiratory passageways, smooth muscle controls:
questions.explanation: Airway smooth muscle adjusts bronchial caliber, widening airways with relaxation and narrowing them with constriction (as in asthma).

questions.stem: Sphincters that regulate the openings of hollow organs are composed of:
questions.explanation: Circular arrangements of smooth muscle form sphincters, controlling passage between organ segments through slow, sustained contraction.

questions.stem: In the absence of sarcomeres, smooth muscle myofilaments attach to:
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle actin filaments anchor to dense bodies (the functional analog of Z-lines), transmitting force across the cell as it contracts.

questions.stem: The ability of vascular smooth muscle to hold contraction for long periods without fatigue is essential for:
options: Maintaining stable vascular tone and blood pressure
questions.explanation: Persistent, low-energy contraction maintains constant vessel caliber — the basis of stable vascular resistance and blood pressure.

questions.stem: Excessive constriction of vascular smooth muscle produces:
questions.explanation: When VSM constricts excessively, resistance rises and blood pressure climbs; focal spasm (e.g., Prinzmetal angina) can even occlude coronary flow.

questions.stem: Peristaltic contractions along the intestinal wall are an example of smooth muscle:
questions.explanation: Sequential contraction waves move intraluminal contents aborally — the classic propulsive function of smooth muscle.

questions.stem: The nucleus of a smooth muscle cell is:
options: Located at the cell periphery in groups
questions.explanation: Each smooth muscle cell has a single nucleus located centrally within its spindle-shaped body.

questions.stem: Caliber control of the vessel lumen belongs to which vascular layer?
questions.explanation: The tunica media contains the vascular smooth muscle that constricts or dilates the vessel, controlling lumen diameter.

questions.stem: Which of the following can initiate smooth muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle is highly responsive: autonomic nerves, hormones (e.g., angiotensin, vasopressin), and local factors (stretch, metabolites, endothelial signals) all regulate its contraction.

questions.stem: The microscopic appearance of smooth muscle is distinguished from skeletal muscle by its:
questions.explanation: Without sarcomere-level alignment of actin and myosin, smooth muscle lacks the banded (striated) pattern seen in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

questions.stem: Relaxation of arterial smooth muscle produces:
options: Decreased vessel radius and increased resistance
Decreased blood pressure through increased vessel radius
questions.explanation: Vasodilation widens the lumen, lowering resistance and therefore blood pressure — the hemodynamic basis of antihypertensive vasodilators.

questions.stem: A patient presents with episodic digital ischemia from intense focal arterial constriction. This symptom reflects:
questions.explanation: Localized, excessive VSM constriction (vasospasm) can critically narrow vessels — the mechanism in vasospastic conditions such as Raynaud phenomenon or Prinzmetal angina.

questions.stem: Drugs that relax vascular smooth muscle will:
questions.explanation: Vasodilators reduce vascular resistance (afterload) and lower blood pressure — used in hypertension, heart failure, and vasospastic disease.

questions.stem: The vascular layer specifically composed of smooth muscle is the:
questions.explanation: The tunica media is the muscular middle layer; the intima is endothelial lining and the adventitia is supportive connective tissue. ---

questions.stem: Intercalated discs contain which two specialized junction types?
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs house desmosomes (mechanical anchoring) and gap junctions (electrical conduction), giving the disc both structural and communicative roles.

questions.stem: The function of desmosomes within intercalated discs is to:
options: Anchor adjacent cells together, preventing separation during contraction
questions.explanation: Desmosomes are mechanical "rivets" that hold myocytes together as they contract, preventing the cells from pulling apart under repetitive force.

questions.stem: The function of gap junctions within intercalated discs is to:
options: Allow ions to pass between cells, conducting the electrical impulse
questions.explanation: Gap junctions form low-resistance channels for ion flow, allowing the action potential to spread rapidly from myocyte to myocyte.

questions.stem: Gap junctions are best described as:
options: Low-resistance pathways for electrical current between cells
questions.explanation: By providing low-resistance intercellular pathways, gap junctions let depolarization current spread directly from one cell to the next.

questions.stem: Because all myocytes are electrically coupled, the heart contracts:
options: As a single functional unit (functional syncytium)
questions.explanation: Electrical coupling through gap junctions makes the atria and ventricles behave as coordinated functional syncytia — each contracting as one unit.

questions.stem: Adjacent cardiac myocytes are connected by:
options: Specialized cell membranes called intercalated discs
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs are the specialized end-to-end cell membrane junctions that connect individual myocytes into a branching network.

questions.stem: The arrangement of cardiac myocytes is best described as:
options: A branching, interconnected network of cells
questions.explanation: Myocytes branch and interconnect, creating a meshwork that transmits force and electrical signals in three dimensions.

questions.stem: The typical number of nuclei in a cardiac myocyte is:
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes usually contain a single nucleus, occasionally two — in contrast to multinucleated skeletal fibers.

questions.stem: "Autorhythmicity" means that:
options: The heart's rhythm is set entirely by the brain
Electrical impulses are generated within the muscle itself
Only the ventricles can pace the heart
questions.explanation: Specialized cardiac cells (like the SA node) spontaneously depolarize, so impulses arise within the heart itself rather than from external nerves.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the autonomic nervous system and cardiac contraction?
options: The ANS modifies the rate and force of cardiac contractions but does not initiate them
The ANS has no influence on the heart
The ANS can voluntarily stop the heart at will
questions.explanation: Because the heart is autorhythmic, ANS input (sympathetic/parasympathetic) tunes rate and contractility — it does not create the impulse.

questions.stem: Without desmosomes, the most likely mechanical consequence during repeated contractions would be:
options: Separation of adjacent myocytes under contraction forces
questions.explanation: Desmosomes anchor cells together; without them, the mechanical stress of repeated contraction would pull myocytes apart.

questions.stem: Which intercalated disc component conducts the electrical impulse?
questions.explanation: Gap junctions carry ionic current between cells; desmosomes serve only mechanical attachment.

questions.stem: In cardiac muscle, the electrical impulse originates:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is self-excitatory: its impulses arise intrinsically (autorhythmic cells) and are then modified by the ANS.

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle is histologically:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle shows light striations (sarcomeres present but less densely organized) and its signature intercalated discs.

questions.stem: Individual cardiac myocytes connect to form:
options: A branching network of interconnected cells
questions.explanation: The branching network architecture allows force and impulses to travel in multiple directions — essential for a wringing ejection motion.

questions.stem: Regarding fatigue, cardiac muscle:
options: Does not fatigue under normal conditions
questions.explanation: The heart contracts rhythmically for a lifetime without functional fatigue, thanks to its aerobic metabolism and rhythmically paced contraction.

questions.stem: Cardiac myocytes are composed of bundles of:
questions.explanation: Within each myocyte, bundles of myofibrils run longitudinally; each myofibril contains the contractile myofilaments.

questions.stem: The layer of the heart wall composed of cardiac muscle is the:
questions.explanation: The myocardium is the thick muscular middle layer made of cardiac muscle; the endocardium is the endothelial lining and the epicardium the outer serous layer.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones can modify cardiac contractile activity?
questions.explanation: Circulating catecholamines (epinephrine) and thyroid hormone are classic modulators of cardiac rate and contractility, acting alongside ANS input.

questions.stem: The specialized cell membrane junction that both anchors myocytes and transmits impulses is the:
questions.explanation: The intercalated disc combines mechanical (desmosomes) and electrical (gap junctions) functions in one structure. ---
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle fibers are:
options: Long, cylindrical, multinucleated, and heavily striated
questions.explanation: Skeletal fibers are long cylinders with many nuclei and dense sarcomere organization, specialized for powerful, voluntary, rapid contraction.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: A "myocyte" is:
questions.explanation: Myocyte is the generic term for a muscle cell; cardiac myocytes are the working cells of the myocardium.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Within a muscle cell, the contractile organelles are organized into:
options: Myofibrils — bundles running the length of the cell
questions.explanation: Each myocyte contains longitudinally arranged bundles of myofibrils, each composed of serially repeating sarcomeres.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Myofibrils are composed of:
questions.explanation: Myofibrils contain myofilaments — the thin (actin) and thick (myosin) filaments that interact to generate force.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle contraction is:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is consciously controlled: motor nerves carry volitional commands from the cortex to the muscle fibers.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Which muscle type contracts and relaxes rapidly but fatigues quickly?
questions.explanation: Rapid contraction–relaxation cycles with quick fatigue characterize skeletal muscle, appropriate for movement but not for sustained work.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The multinucleation of skeletal fibers results from:
options: Nuclear division without cell division in adults
Developmental mitosis occurring without cytoplasmic division
questions.explanation: Embryonic myoblasts divide their nuclei without dividing the cytoplasm, producing long multinucleated fibers.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Striations in skeletal muscle directly reflect:
options: The organized arrangement of actin and myosin into sarcomeres
questions.explanation: The repeating banding pattern is the light-microscopic image of aligned sarcomeres within parallel myofibrils.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The primary function of skeletal muscle is:
options: Producing movement at joints by acting on bones
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle attaches to bones across joints; its contractions produce movement and maintain posture.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Within the cardiac myocyte, the contractile units are bundled into:
questions.explanation: The myocyte contains bundles of myofibrils; each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres — the actual contractile machinery.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The cytoplasm of a muscle cell is called:
questions.explanation: Sarcoplasm is the muscle cell's cytoplasm; the sarcolemma is its membrane, and the SR is its calcium-handling organelle.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The cell membrane of a muscle fiber is termed the:
questions.explanation: The sarcolemma encloses the myocyte and invaginates to form T-tubules that carry the action potential inward.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Which muscle type shows the heaviest striations?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle's densely packed, perfectly aligned sarcomeres produce the heaviest striations; cardiac striation is lighter, and smooth muscle is non-striated.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The contraction–relaxation pattern of skeletal muscle is:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is built for speed: fast contraction and relaxation cycles that fatigue relatively quickly.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Which muscle type is self-excitatory?
questions.explanation: Only cardiac muscle generates its own electrical impulses; skeletal requires nervous activation, and smooth responds to nerves, hormones, and local factors.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The correct hierarchical organization of cardiac muscle, from largest to smallest, is:
questions.explanation: Myocytes contain myofibrils, which contain myofilaments organized into sarcomeres — each level nested within the next.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: The number of nuclei in a typical cardiac myocyte is:
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are typically mononucleated, occasionally binucleated — never multinucleated like skeletal fibers.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Voluntary control of skeletal muscle is exerted by the:
questions.explanation: Conscious commands descend from the motor cortex through nerves to stimulate skeletal muscle fibers.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: Which statement about cardiac muscle control is true?
options: It is controlled consciously during exercise
It is controlled by skeletal motor nerves
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle contraction is involuntary; even though impulses arise internally, we cannot consciously direct them.
tags: Skeletal Muscle and Myocyte Internal Organization

questions.stem: How many types of muscle tissue exist in the body?
questions.explanation: Three: skeletal, cardiac, and smooth — distinguished by location, shape, control, striation, and fatigue behavior. ---

questions.stem: The sarcomere is defined as the segment between two:
questions.explanation: One sarcomere extends from one Z-line (Z-disk) to the next — the repeating basic contractile unit of the myofibril.

questions.stem: The thick filaments of the sarcomere are composed of:
questions.explanation: Myosin forms the thick filament; its heads (with ATPase activity) form the cross-bridges that pull the thin filaments.

questions.stem: The thin filaments of the sarcomere are composed of:
questions.explanation: Thin filaments consist mainly of actin along with the regulatory proteins tropomyosin and troponin.

questions.stem: Each cardiac thick filament contains approximately how many myosin molecules?
questions.explanation: Roughly 300 myosin molecules assemble into each thick filament, with heads projecting outward for cross-bridge formation.

questions.stem: Titin is best described as:
options: An elastic protein connecting myosin to the Z-line, maintaining sarcomere integrity
The membrane channel that admits calcium
questions.explanation: Titin spans from the Z-line to the myosin filament, acting as a molecular spring that maintains sarcomere structural integrity and passive elasticity.

questions.stem: Sarcomere shortening occurs through:
options: Shortening of the myosin molecules themselves
Interaction (sliding) between actin and myosin filaments
questions.explanation: Cross-bridge cycling slides thin filaments toward the sarcomere center; the filaments themselves do not shorten — the sarcomere does.

questions.stem: One Z-line to the next Z-line spans exactly:
questions.explanation: The sarcomere's boundaries are defined by adjacent Z-lines; thousands repeat in series along each myofibril.

questions.stem: During contraction, the relationship between actin and myosin is that they:
questions.explanation: Myosin heads bind actin and pull, generating the sliding interaction that shortens the sarcomere.

questions.stem: The myosin heads possess which enzymatic activity?
questions.explanation: Myosin heads are ATPases: hydrolysis of ATP energizes the head for the power stroke of contraction.

questions.stem: The process that drives the actin–myosin interaction is:
questions.explanation: Excitation–contraction coupling links the electrical action potential to calcium release, which then permits and drives the actin–myosin interaction.

questions.stem: The basic contractile unit of the myocyte is the:
questions.explanation: The sarcomere — Z-line to Z-line — is the fundamental unit: all macroscopic contraction is the summed shortening of millions of sarcomeres.

questions.stem: Beyond structure, the functional contribution of titin includes:
options: Providing passive elastic recoil that helps the sarcomere return to resting length
questions.explanation: Titin's spring-like elasticity opposes overstretch and assists recoil toward resting sarcomere length during relaxation.

questions.stem: Z-lines, myosin filaments, actin filaments, and titin are all components of the:
questions.explanation: All these elements reside within the sarcomere, the organized repeating unit that produces striations and contraction.

questions.stem: Which filament pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Actin composes the thin filament; myosin composes the thick filament.

questions.stem: In series along a myofibril, sarcomeres are separated and delimited by:
questions.explanation: Thousands of sarcomeres lie end-to-end, each delimited by a Z-line shared with its neighbor.

questions.stem: The sliding filament mechanism means that during contraction:
options: Thick and thin filaments slide past each other, reducing sarcomere length
questions.explanation: Cross-bridge cycling pulls the filaments toward each other; filament lengths stay constant while the sarcomere shortens.

questions.stem: As a sarcomere shortens, the Z-lines:
questions.explanation: Sliding of actin toward the center draws the Z-lines toward each other, reducing the sarcomere's length.

questions.stem: Titin's physical span within the sarcomere runs from:
options: The Z-line to the myosin filament
questions.explanation: Titin anchors at the Z-line and extends to the thick (myosin) filament, tethering the sarcomere's architecture.

questions.stem: The visible striated banding of cardiac and skeletal muscle corresponds to:
questions.explanation: A-bands, I-bands, and Z-lines of aligned sarcomeres create the striated pattern under the microscope.

questions.stem: Because sarcomeres are arranged in series along a myofibril, their individual shortenings:
options: Sum to produce shortening of the entire myofibril and myocyte
questions.explanation: Serial sarcomeres shorten in concert, multiplying the total contraction along the myofibril — the basis of macroscopic muscle shortening. ---
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The thin filament is composed of:
options: Actin plus regulatory proteins (tropomyosin and troponin)
questions.explanation: Thin filaments contain the contractile protein actin plus the regulatory proteins that control access of myosin to the actin binding sites.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: Troponin T (TnT) has the specific role of:
options: Anchoring the troponin complex to tropomyosin
questions.explanation: TnT is the anchoring subunit that tethers the troponin complex to the tropomyosin strand on the thin filament.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The troponin subunit that binds calcium and triggers contraction is:
questions.explanation: TnC is the calcium-binding subunit; its binding of Ca²⁺ initiates the conformational change that starts contraction.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The troponin subunit that inhibits the actin–myosin interaction at rest is:
questions.explanation: TnI is the inhibitory subunit: at rest it holds the actin–myosin interaction "off" until calcium removes the brake.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The immediate chemical energy that powers contraction comes from:
questions.explanation: Myosin ATPase hydrolyzes ATP to energize the myosin head; ATP is the immediate fuel for cross-bridge cycling.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The projections of the myosin filament that bind to actin are called:
questions.explanation: Myosin heads project from the thick filament, forming cross-bridges with actin binding sites during contraction.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: Troponin and tropomyosin are located on the:
questions.explanation: The regulatory proteins sit on the thin (actin) filament, where they control exposure of the myosin binding sites.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: ATP is required during contraction specifically for:
questions.explanation: ATP energizes the myosin head (via its ATPase) and is also needed for cross-bridge detachment — without it, cycling stops.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: At rest, which protein covers the actin binding sites and blocks cross-bridge formation?
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin lies in the groove of the actin helix, physically covering the myosin binding sites until calcium signaling moves it aside.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The troponin complex consists of how many subunits?
questions.explanation: Three subunits: TnT (anchors to tropomyosin), TnI (inhibits at rest), and TnC (binds calcium).
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: Clinically, the cardiac troponin proteins are important because they:
options: Serve as serum biomarkers of myocardial injury
questions.explanation: Troponin released from damaged myocytes (e.g., in MI) is measured in serum as the primary biomarker of myocardial necrosis.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The number of myosin molecules per cardiac thick filament is approximately:
questions.explanation: About 300 myosin molecules assemble into each thick filament — a structural fact with functional relevance to force generation.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: After ATP hydrolysis, the energized myosin head performs the:
options: Power stroke, pulling the actin filament
questions.explanation: The energized head swings (power stroke) after binding actin, dragging the thin filament toward the sarcomere center.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The actin binding sites become exposed for myosin when:
options: Calcium binds TnC, removing the TnI inhibition
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ binding to TnC induces a conformational change that releases TnI's inhibition and shifts tropomyosin, exposing the binding sites.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The regulatory protein that must physically move to expose actin's binding sites is:
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin strands slide deeper into the actin groove upon the calcium–troponin signal, uncovering the cross-bridge binding sites.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: Cross-bridge cycling requires ATP at which points?
options: For both head energization and detachment
questions.explanation: ATP is hydrolyzed to energize the head and must bind again to detach the head from actin; cycling ceases without it.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: Which troponin subunit is inhibitory at rest?
questions.explanation: TnI holds contraction off; calcium binding to TnC neutralizes TnI's inhibition, permitting cross-bridge formation.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The "trigger" ion for contraction binds directly to:
questions.explanation: Calcium is the trigger and its receptor is TnC; without this binding, tropomyosin stays in the blocking position.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: Tropomyosin's position on the thin filament is:
options: Running along the groove of the actin double helix
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin lies lengthwise in the helical groove of actin, ideally positioned to block or reveal successive binding sites.
tags: Thick and Thin Filaments — Contractile and Regulatory Proteins

questions.stem: The thin filaments are anchored at:
questions.explanation: Actin filaments extend from the Z-lines toward the sarcomere center, defining the I-bands on either side of the Z-disk. ---
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Excitation–contraction coupling is the process that links:
options: Electrical excitation (action potential) to mechanical contraction
questions.explanation: ECC converts the myocyte's electrical signal into the calcium signal that produces mechanical shortening — the essential translation of ECG to pump function.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The membrane of the cardiac myocyte is the:
questions.explanation: The sarcolemma is the myocyte's cell membrane; it propagates the action potential and invaginates to form T-tubules.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: T-tubules are formed by:
questions.explanation: T-tubules are tubular inpouchings of the surface membrane (sarcolemma) that carry the action potential into the cell interior and open to the extracellular space.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Because T-tubules open to the extracellular space, they serve as the site of:
options: Ion exchange between the extracellular fluid and the myocyte interior
questions.explanation: Being continuous with the extracellular space, T-tubules bring ion channels into close contact with the SR, enabling rapid calcium-triggered excitation.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) primarily functions in:
options: Calcium control — storing, releasing, and resequestering Ca²⁺
questions.explanation: The SR is the myocyte's calcium reservoir: it releases Ca²⁺ to trigger contraction and reuptakes it to permit relaxation.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The correct sequence of excitation–contraction coupling is:
options: Calcium release → action potential → T-tubule depolarization
Action potential → T-tubule conduction → SR calcium release → contraction
SR calcium release → T-tubule depolarization → action potential
questions.explanation: The action potential spreads along the sarcolemma into T-tubules, triggering SR calcium release, which then activates the contractile machinery.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The functional coupling complex formed by a T-tubule and adjacent SR is called a:
options: Diad (in cardiac muscle; triad in skeletal muscle)
questions.explanation: In cardiac muscle, a T-tubule pairs with one SR terminal cisterna (a diad); skeletal muscle uses triads — both arrangements position calcium release next to the contractile filaments.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Calcium released from the SR initiates contraction by binding to:
options: Troponin C on the thin filament
questions.explanation: SR-released calcium binds TnC, relieving inhibition and allowing tropomyosin movement and cross-bridge formation.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Myocardial relaxation requires:
options: Active reuptake of calcium into the SR (an ATP-dependent process)
questions.explanation: Relaxation is active: SR calcium pumps (ATP-driven) clear Ca²⁺ from the cytosol, tropomyosin re-covers the binding sites, and cross-bridges release.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The structure that conducts the action potential from the cell surface into the myocyte interior is the:
questions.explanation: T-tubules are sarcolemma invaginations that carry depolarization rapidly to the cell's core, ensuring synchronous SR calcium release.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The purpose of sarcolemmal invagination (T-tubules) is to:
options: Increase the cell's surface area for metabolism
Allow the impulse to reach deep myofilaments quickly and uniformly
questions.explanation: Without T-tubules, depolarization would reach the cell center by slow diffusion; the invaginations make contraction of deep and superficial sarcomeres nearly simultaneous.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Which organelle is responsible for calcium control in the myocyte?
questions.explanation: The SR stores, releases, and resequesters calcium — making it the central regulator of the contraction–relaxation cycle.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Excitation–contraction coupling literally converts:
options: An electrical signal into a mechanical event (shortening)
questions.explanation: The action potential (electrical) is coupled through calcium to cross-bridge cycling (mechanical) — the definition of ECC.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The site of ion exchange between the extracellular space and the myocyte interior during excitation is the:
questions.explanation: Because T-tubules are open to the extracellular space, ion flux (including the calcium that triggers SR release) occurs across their membranes.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The calcium that activates contraction comes from:
options: SR release supplemented by a small influx across the sarcolemma/T-tubule
questions.explanation: Most activator calcium is released from the SR, triggered by a small "trigger" calcium influx through T-tubule channels — a positive-feedback concept known as calcium-induced calcium release.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Relaxation of the myocyte begins when:
options: Calcium is removed from the cytosol (reuptaken into the SR), allowing tropomyosin to re-cover the binding sites
questions.explanation: As cytosolic calcium falls, troponin returns to its inhibitory configuration, cross-bridges detach, and the sarcomere lengthens passively.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: Calcium-induced calcium release refers to:
options: The small T-tubule calcium influx triggering the SR to release a much larger amount of calcium
Calcium leaving through the sarcolemma only
questions.explanation: Trigger calcium entering through L-type channels stimulates SR release channels, amplifying the signal ~10-fold — the amplification step of cardiac ECC.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: In cardiac muscle, the T-tubules are characteristically located at the level of the:
questions.explanation: Cardiac T-tubules sit at the Z-line (unlike skeletal muscle, where they sit at the A–I junction), positioning calcium release near the sarcomere ends.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: A heart that generates normal electrical impulses but cannot couple them to contraction would:
options: Have a normal ECG with no effective mechanical pumping (electromechanical dissociation)
questions.explanation: ECC failure (e.g., profound hypoxia, hyperkalemia, calcium dysfunction) produces electrical activity without mechanical output — pulseless electrical activity on the monitor.
tags: Excitation–Contraction Coupling — Sarcolemma, T-Tubules, and Sarcoplasmic Reticulum

questions.stem: The SERCA pump of the sarcoplasmic reticulum functions to:
options: Reuptake (resequester) calcium into the SR during relaxation
questions.explanation: SERCA (SR Ca²⁺-ATPase) actively pumps cytosolic calcium back into the SR, an ATP-dependent step essential for relaxation (lusitropy). ---
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: ATP is consumed during contraction primarily by:
options: The myosin ATPase powering cross-bridge cycling
questions.explanation: Myosin heads hydrolyze ATP to energize and cycle; this is the largest direct ATP consumer during systole.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The contraction cycle is switched on when:
options: Calcium binds troponin C, relieving TnI inhibition
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺–TnC binding is the "on switch"; it releases the inhibition and shifts tropomyosin off the actin binding sites.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: If ATP is completely unavailable to the myosin head, cross-bridges:
options: Cannot detach, producing a rigor-like locked state
questions.explanation: Detachment requires ATP binding; without it, heads remain locked on actin (rigor), as occurs in severe ischemia and post-mortem rigor mortis.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The chief ATP-generating pathway of the working cardiac myocyte is:
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are packed with mitochondria (~30–40% of cell volume) and depend almost entirely on oxidative phosphorylation — hence their oxygen sensitivity.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The abundance of mitochondria in cardiac myocytes reflects:
options: Their need for continuous aerobic ATP production
questions.explanation: A heart that beats ~100,000 times a day cannot rely on anaerobic metabolism; mitochondrial density underpins its fatigue resistance and oxygen dependence.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: Relaxation of the myocardium is:
options: Entirely passive with no energy cost
questions.explanation: Clearing cytosolic calcium (SR pumps, sarcolemmal extrusion) requires ATP; impaired relaxation is an early feature of ischemia and diastolic dysfunction.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The correct order of the cross-bridge cycle is:
questions.explanation: The energized head attaches to actin, executes the power stroke, detaches when fresh ATP binds, and is re-energized by hydrolysis for the next cycle.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The contraction phase of the cardiac cycle corresponds to the cellular period of:
options: Elevated cytosolic calcium with active cross-bridge cycling
questions.explanation: Systole is the cellular picture of high cytosolic Ca²⁺ and cross-bridge activity; diastole is the calcium-cleared, inhibited state.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: Cytosolic calcium is cleared after contraction mainly by:
options: SR reuptake (SERCA), with some extrusion across the sarcolemma
questions.explanation: SERCA resequesters most calcium into the SR; a smaller amount exits via the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger and sarcolemmal pump.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: In myocardial ischemia, the combination of low ATP and impaired calcium handling causes:
options: Reduced systolic contraction and impaired (delayed) relaxation
questions.explanation: Energy starvation weakens both contraction (less cross-bridge work) and relaxation (poor calcium clearance) — the cellular basis of ischemic systolic and diastolic dysfunction.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The correct intracellular contraction cascade is:
options: Calcium → TnC → release of TnI inhibition → tropomyosin shifts → actin–myosin interaction
questions.explanation: Calcium binds TnC, TnI's inhibition is lifted, tropomyosin moves off the binding sites, and cross-bridges form — the canonical sequence.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The myosin head uses ATP by:
options: Hydrolyzing it via its ATPase site to "cock" the head into the high-energy position
questions.explanation: ATP hydrolysis energizes (cocks) the myosin head; the stored energy is released in the power stroke upon actin binding.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: A patient with severe coronary stenosis develops transient LV "stiffness" and elevated filling pressures during angina. The cellular explanation is:
options: Impaired relaxation from ATP-starved calcium reuptake (ischemic diastolic dysfunction)
Excess sarcolemmal calcium influx improving relaxation
questions.explanation: Without ATP, SERCA cannot clear calcium promptly; diastolic Ca²⁺ remains elevated and the ventricle relaxes poorly — raising filling pressures during ischemia.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The ion directly responsible for switching contraction on is:
questions.explanation: Calcium is the universal contraction trigger in striated muscle; sodium and potassium mainly set the membrane potential.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: Systolic pump strength depends most directly on:
options: The amount of calcium delivered to the contractile apparatus during each beat
questions.explanation: More calcium released and available to troponin recruits more cross-bridges — the cellular basis of inotropy (and of positive inotropic drugs that raise calcium availability).
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: "Lusitropy" refers to:
options: The rate and completeness of myocardial relaxation
questions.explanation: Lusitropy is relaxation (diastolic function), driven mainly by SERCA-mediated calcium reuptake; enhanced by sympathetic stimulation, impaired by ischemia.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: A cross-bridge detaches from actin when:
options: A fresh ATP molecule binds the myosin head
questions.explanation: ATP binding to myosin reduces its affinity for actin, allowing detachment — without ATP the bridge stays locked.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: Sympathetic (β1) stimulation improves both systole and diastole because it:
options: Increases calcium influx and SR calcium uptake, enhancing inotropy (stronger contraction) and lusitropy (faster relaxation)
questions.explanation: β1 stimulation raises trigger calcium (stronger systole) and speeds SERCA reuptake (faster diastolic relaxation) — allowing high heart rates without incomplete relaxation.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: Digoxin increases contractility at the cellular level by:
options: Raising intracellular calcium availability (inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, secondarily reducing calcium extrusion)
questions.explanation: By inhibiting Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, digoxin raises intracellular Na⁺, which reduces the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger's calcium removal — leaving more calcium for the contractile machinery.
tags: Calcium Handling, ATP, and the Contraction–Relaxation Cycle

questions.stem: The heart's total ATP expenditure each beat includes:
options: Cross-bridge cycling plus ion pumping (SERCA, Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase, and other homeostatic pumps)
questions.explanation: Contraction work and the ion-pumping required to restore the resting state (including SERCA) together consume the myocyte's ATP each cycle. ---
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Vascular smooth muscle (VSM) is located in which layer of the vessel wall?
questions.explanation: The tunica media houses the smooth muscle that controls vessel caliber; the intima is endothelium and the adventitia is supporting connective tissue.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: The three layers of the vessel wall, from innermost to outermost, are:
questions.explanation: Intima (endothelial lining), media (smooth muscle), adventitia (outer support/anchoring) — the standard trilaminar organization.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Vascular smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction) causes:
options: Increased resistance and increased blood pressure
questions.explanation: Narrowing the lumen raises resistance; since pressure = flow × resistance, vasoconstriction elevates blood pressure.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Vascular smooth muscle relaxation (vasodilation) causes:
options: Decreased resistance and decreased blood pressure
questions.explanation: A wider lumen lowers resistance and pressure — the mechanism of vasodilator therapy and of physiologic hyperemia.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Which vessel wall layer provides structural support and anchoring?
questions.explanation: The outer adventitia (mostly connective tissue) anchors the vessel to surrounding structures and supports the wall.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: The endothelial lining of the vessel wall resides in the:
questions.explanation: The intima is the innermost layer, a single layer of squamous endothelial cells in direct contact with blood.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Arteries are distinguished from veins by:
options: A thicker media with more smooth muscle
The presence of valves in the lumen
questions.explanation: Arterial walls are thicker and more muscular to withstand and modulate higher pressures; veins are thinner, more compliant, and contain valves.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Compared with cardiac muscle, vascular smooth muscle:
options: Contains actin and myosin but lacks organized sarcomeres
questions.explanation: VSM contracts via actin–myosin interactions but without sarcomere-level organization — hence it is non-striated.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: The contraction pattern of VSM is ideally suited to its role because it:
options: Contracts slowly and sustains tone without fatigue
questions.explanation: Sustained low-energy tone maintains constant vessel caliber for hours to days — impossible for fatigable skeletal-type muscle.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: By adjusting the diameter of different vascular beds, VSM performs the crucial function of:
options: Redistributing blood flow to where it is needed
questions.explanation: Differential constriction/dilation shunts cardiac output among organs (e.g., to muscle during exercise, gut during digestion) without changing total output.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Chronic excessive VSM constriction systemically would be expected to cause:
questions.explanation: Persistently elevated vascular resistance from excessive vasoconstriction produces systemic hypertension.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Excessive systemic vasodilation (as in sepsis) causes:
questions.explanation: Vasodilation collapses resistance; blood pressure falls despite a hyperdynamic heart — the hemodynamics of distributive (septic) shock.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: The vessels where VSM tone exerts the greatest control over resistance are the:
questions.explanation: Arterioles are the chief resistance vessels; their muscular tone sets regional resistance and pressure drop.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: The layer that contains the smooth muscle responsible for caliber control is the:
questions.explanation: The tunica media is the muscular layer; its VSM is the effector of vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Vascular smooth muscle tone is regulated by:
options: Autonomic nerves, circulating hormones, and local factors
questions.explanation: VSM is governed by sympathetic nerves (constrictor tone), hormones (angiotensin II, vasopressin, epinephrine), and local metabolites/endothelial signals.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: Capillaries differ from arteries and veins in that they:
options: Lack a smooth muscle layer, consisting essentially of a single endothelial layer
questions.explanation: Capillaries are essentially endothelial tubes optimized for exchange; resistance control is exercised upstream at the arterioles.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: A localized weakening of the tunica media in a major artery can result in:
options: An aneurysm (bulging from loss of wall support)
questions.explanation: The media provides wall strength; its weakening (e.g., hypertension, Marfan, syphilis) allows progressive bulging — an aneurysm.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: The largest amount of VSM relative to lumen size is found in:
questions.explanation: Arteries have proportionally thick muscular walls (the "thicker, more muscle" rule from the lecture), and arterioles carry the highest resistance function.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: "Vascular tone" is best described as:
options: The passive elasticity of the aorta only
The baseline state of partial VSM constriction, which can be increased or decreased
The heart rate set by the SA node
questions.explanation: Vessels maintain a baseline tone; neurally and humorally modulated increases/decreases in tone produce vasoconstriction or vasodilation.
tags: Vascular Smooth Muscle and the Vessel Wall

questions.stem: In septic shock, the hemodynamic picture of excessive vasodilation includes:
options: Elevated afterload with low cardiac output
Low systemic vascular resistance with hypotension
questions.explanation: Pathologic vasodilation drops SVR; blood pressure falls despite high cardiac output — distributive shock's defining profile. ---
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: The endothelium is composed of:
options: A single layer of squamous cells lining all vessels
questions.explanation: The endothelium is a one-cell-thick squamous lining continuous throughout the vascular tree, in direct contact with circulating blood.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: The endothelial lining of the heart chambers is called the:
questions.explanation: The endocardium is the heart's inner endothelial lining, continuous with the vessel intima — one continuous surface from heart to capillaries.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: The endothelium is continuous:
options: From the heart through all arteries, capillaries, and veins
questions.explanation: Endothelium forms an unbroken lining from the heart chambers through the entire vascular circuit — vascular "plumbing" with one continuous surface.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: A principal function of the endothelium is to:
options: Regulate vasodilation and vasoconstriction (e.g., via nitric oxide)
questions.explanation: Endothelial cells release vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) and constrictors (endothelin), tuning vessel tone in response to flow and metabolic signals.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Endothelial cells participate in hemostasis by:
options: Controlling clotting and platelet function (pro-coagulant and anti-coagulant balance)
questions.explanation: The endothelium normally presents an anti-thrombotic surface but can become pro-coagulant when injured — central to thrombosis on disrupted plaques.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Endothelial roles in immune function include:
options: Modulating inflammatory responses and leukocyte trafficking
questions.explanation: Endothelium expresses adhesion molecules and secretes inflammatory mediators, directing leukocyte movement during inflammation.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: The classic endothelium-derived vasodilating mediator is:
questions.explanation: NO released by endothelial cells relaxes VSM (vasodilation); endothelin-1 is the counterpart vasoconstrictor.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Endothelial dysfunction is a central early event in:
questions.explanation: Loss of normal endothelial vasodilator/anti-thrombotic function promotes lipid infiltration, inflammation, and plaque formation — the initiation of atherosclerosis.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Capillary endothelium is structurally suited to its exchange role because it is:
options: Extremely thin, facilitating exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste
questions.explanation: A single-cell-thick wall minimizes diffusion distance — the structural basis of capillary exchange.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the endothelium?
questions.explanation: Sarcomere shortening is the myocyte's job. The endothelium regulates vascular tone, hemostasis, and inflammation.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: According to the lecture's key takeaways, contraction of the heart is driven by:
questions.explanation: Calcium is the trigger and ATP the fuel: "Calcium + ATP drive contraction" is the cellular engine room of every heartbeat.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: The phrase "electrical → mechanical coupling" summarizes:
options: Excitation–contraction coupling: the action potential becomes contraction via calcium
questions.explanation: ECC is literally the conversion of electrical excitation into mechanical shortening — the bridge between ECG and pump function.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: After a myocardial infarction, regional wall motion abnormality develops because:
options: Necrotic myocytes cannot execute excitation–contraction coupling, so the affected region does not shorten
questions.explanation: Dead myocytes lose contractile machinery; the infarct zone is akinetic or dyskinetic while surviving myocardium compensates — the echo signature of MI.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized pathologically by:
options: Disorganized, hypertrophied sarcomeres/myocytes producing a stiff, thick wall
questions.explanation: Mutations in sarcomere proteins cause myocyte disarray and hypertrophy — thick, stiff walls with diastolic dysfunction and outflow obstruction.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Because cardiac myocytes form an electrical syncytium, an impulse arising anywhere in the atrial muscle:
options: Spreads through gap junctions to excite the atria as a single unit
questions.explanation: Low-resistance gap junctions propagate the impulse cell-to-cell, so the whole chamber contracts as a unit — the syncytium concept.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Infective endocarditis is an infection of the:
questions.explanation: The endocardium is the heart's endothelial lining; damaged valve endothelium can seed infection with vegetations.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Age-related arterial stiffening is largely attributable to changes in the:
options: Media — loss of elastic recoil and altered VSM/connective tissue
questions.explanation: Medial degeneration (elastin fragmentation, collagen deposition, VSM changes) stiffens arteries, raising systolic pressure and afterload with age.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: On echocardiography, longstanding hypertension appears as thickened LV walls because:
options: Myocytes add sarcomeres (hypertrophy) in response to chronic pressure load
questions.explanation: Individual myocytes enlarge (add sarcomeres in parallel), thickening the wall — the cellular substrate of concentric LVH seen on echo.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces a contraction from impulse to shortening?
options: SR calcium → impulse → gap junction → actin–myosin
Impulse → gap junctions → T-tubules → SR calcium release → calcium binds TnC → actin–myosin interaction → sarcomere shortening
questions.explanation: This is the full ECC cascade: conducted impulse, T-tubular penetration, SR calcium release, troponin activation, cross-bridge cycling, sarcomere shortening.
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration

questions.stem: The final common pathway uniting all cardiac cellular machinery is:
options: Sarcomere shortening through calcium-activated, ATP-fueled actin–myosin interaction
questions.explanation: Whatever the trigger (electrical, hormonal, pharmacologic), the heart's output ultimately comes down to calcium-triggered, ATP-powered sarcomere shortening in millions of myocytes. --- *End of question bank — Lecture 7: Cardiac Cellular Structure and Function. 200 questions.*
tags: Endothelial Cells, Myocardial Metabolism, and Integration
